justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty check. It says `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any SafeSelector placeholder, including attribute selectors, not only hex escapes. When the next character after the separator is a hex char, the combinator is skipped and the selector is scoped incorrectly (e.g. `[disabled] div`). The known bug's `:host[foo]>div` case uses `>` rather than a space, but the mechanism is the same: an attribute placeholder plus a following hex character skips the separator.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The check is too broad. `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any part containing any SafeSelector placeholder, and SafeSelector also creates placeholders for attribute selectors (`[attr=val]`) and for escapes that are not hex escapes (`\:`). It does not check that the part ends in a hex escape. If such a part is followed by a space and a descendant selector starting with a hex character (a-f or 0-9), the combinator is skipped. Examples are `[disabled] div`, `input[type=text] a`, and `.one\:two .abc`. These are no longer split and scoped as separate compound selectors, so the output scoping attributes are wrong (for example `[disabled] div[contenta]` instead of `[disabled][contenta] div[contenta]`). This regresses common selectors.

justification: Finding 0 points at the same faulty check, `part.match(_placeholderRe) && next char is hex`. It says the check is too broad because it matches any `__ph-N__` placeholder, not just one standing for a hex escape. It shows this causes valid separators to be skipped when the next character happens to be a hex digit, and notes it also applies to `>`, `+` and `~`. Its examples use non-hex escapes (`\:`) rather than attribute-selector placeholders. Still, the mechanism is the same: the generic placeholder check fires for placeholders that are not hex escapes. It recommends checking that the placeholder stands for a hex escape, which is essentially the real fix.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The check is too broad. It only tests that the part contains any `__ph-N__` placeholder and that the next character is a hex digit. SafeSelector turns every backslash escape into a placeholder, including non-hex escapes like `\:` and `\/`. So `.md\:flex div {}` or `.sm\:foo a {}` becomes `.md__ph-0__flex div`, the part matches the placeholder, and `d` or `a` passes the hex test. The descendant combinator is then skipped and the selectors are merged. The scoping attribute is not added to the first compound selector, and the combinator handling is wrong. This regresses previously working selectors, such as Tailwind-style classes followed by a descendant starting with a-f or a digit. The check should confirm that the placeholder is at the end of the part and that it stands for a hex escape. It also applies to non-space separators such as `>`, `+` and `~`, where `selector[res.index+1]` is not the separator's trailing character.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It points to the removal of the `if (_global.beforeEach)`/`afterEach` guards in test_hooks.ts, which makes the hooks run unconditionally. It also gives the same failure: "ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined" when the module is loaded outside a test framework, for example when pulled into a bundle.
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally when the module loads. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework defines these globals, for example when the file is pulled into a bundle or loaded in a non-test context, it throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code skipped registration safely in that case.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the removal of the `if (_global.beforeEach)`/`afterEach` guards in test_hooks.ts. It says the hooks are "now called unconditionally at module load" and would throw "ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined" when no test framework is present. That is the same faulty code and failure mechanism as the known bug, and the suggested guard matches the fix.
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework globals exist (for example a server bundle or catalog, or a non-test tool that loads the module), this throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. Previously the module loaded without error in those environments. A `typeof beforeEach !== 'undefined'` guard is needed.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the exact defect. It says `collectDeferredSymbols` "never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport`. It stays at the initial `false`", and that the per-block deps functions therefore emit `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, so the lazily loaded dependency resolves to undefined. This matches the known bug's mechanism and fix. Finding 1 describes a different issue: misclassifying mixed default-plus-named imports.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: `collectDeferredSymbols` sets `deferBlockDep.isDeferrable` and `importPath`, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport`. It stays at the initial `false`. The per-defer-block dependency functions (`TemplateDefinitionBuilder` and `createDeferDepsFns`) read `dep.isDefaultImport`, so for a default-imported component they still emit `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`. At runtime the lazily loaded dependency resolves to `undefined` and the deferred content breaks. Only the `deferrableTypes` map and `setClassMetadataAsync` get the correct `default` access.

`isDefaultImport` is computed per import declaration, not per identifier. `import Cmp, {Other} from './x'` has `namedBindings` set, so the default-imported `Cmp` is treated as a named import and gets `m.Cmp` instead of `m.default`. Conversely, the named `Other` could be misclassified if the check were changed. A mixed import therefore produces an incorrect dynamic-import accessor.

justification: The known bug is that `collectDeferredSymbols` never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects, so they keep `false` and the per-block loader emits `m.CmpA`. Finding [0] instead says the `isDefaultImport()` helper misclassifies mixed imports such as `import CmpA, {CmpB}` and `import {default as CmpA}`. That is a different mechanism in different code: "isDefaultImport() only checks that the import clause has no namedBindings". It does not point to the missing assignment on deferBlockDep.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: isDefaultImport() only checks that the import clause has no namedBindings. For a mixed import such as `import CmpA, {CmpB} from './x'`, namedBindings is defined, so a deferred default-imported symbol is reported as not default. The generated code is then `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. The same failure happens for `import {default as CmpA}`. The check is per declaration and never identifies which binding is the deferred symbol.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says that `{...options}` "copies only own enumerable properties", so `capture`, `once` and `passive` supplied through the prototype chain or as accessors "will silently lose those values". It also notes that "only `signal` is special-cased". This is exactly the known bug's mechanism and the faulty code.
ground_truth: To avoid mutating readonly/frozen listener options, the PR copies them with `{...options}` in `copyEventListenerOptions` before passing them to the native `addEventListener` (special-casing only `signal`). Object spread copies only own enumerable data properties, while the native call reads each option via [[Get]]. Options supplied as getters, on the prototype, or as non-enumerable properties are silently dropped: `capture: true` becomes bubbling, `once: true` fires repeatedly, and the MDN `passive` feature-detection getter is never invoked. Fixed by also reading `capture`, `once`, `passive` and `signal` from the source object when the spread did not copy them.

findings.description: copyEventListenerOptions uses `{...options}`, which copies only own enumerable properties. Options objects that supply `capture`, `once` or `passive` through the prototype chain or as accessors on a class instance (for example `Object.create({capture:true})`) will silently lose those values. Only `signal` is special-cased. The native listener is then registered with different options than the caller asked for. This is an edge-case regression.

justification: Finding 0 is about the inverted constructor condition and the lost tabindex on non-anchor hosts, which is a different defect. Finding 1 says the default-handling clause is inverted, so links get no subscription when the global default is merge/preserve. That is the inverted-clause critique the known bug explicitly excludes. It never says that relative links need the subscription regardless of queryParamsHandling, which is the actual flawed premise.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The constructor condition is inverted: `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { this.subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary(); } else { this.setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0'); }`. For non-anchor elements, the subscribe call returns immediately because it bails when `!isAnchorElement`, and `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` is never called. Non-anchor hosts such as `<div routerLink>` therefore lose their default `tabindex="0"` and become unreachable by keyboard. For anchors, `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl` is a no-op, so the else branch does nothing useful.

The subscription condition is wrong. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes when the link does NOT depend on router state. It skips the subscription when the router-wide `defaultQueryParamsHandling` is 'merge' or 'preserve' and the link sets no handling of its own. In that case the href depends on the current URL's query params but is never updated on NavigationEnd, so the href goes stale after navigation.

justification: Finding 0 is about the inverted anchor/non-anchor condition affecting tabindex, which is a different defect. Finding 1 says the default-handling clause is inverted ("The `!` before `dependsOnRouterState` should be removed"). The known bug explicitly excludes this: that fix would subscribe in fewer cases, which is the opposite of the real fix. Neither finding identifies that relative links need the subscription regardless of query or fragment handling.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The constructor condition was inverted. The original code subscribed for anchor elements and called `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` for non-anchor elements. Now `if (!this.isAnchorElement)` calls `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary()`, which returns immediately for non-anchors, so it does nothing. The `else` branch then sets `tabindex="0"` on anchor elements and never on non-anchor elements. Non-anchor `routerLink` hosts such as `<div routerLink>` lose their default tabindex and are no longer keyboard-focusable. Native anchors get an unwanted tabindex.

The subscription condition for the case with no `queryParamsHandling` is inverted. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes to NavigationEnd when the default handling does NOT depend on router state. It skips subscribing when the router default is 'merge' or 'preserve', which is when the href does depend on the current query params. In that case the href goes stale after navigation. The `!` before `dependsOnRouterState` should be removed.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty code and the same mechanism. It notes that `first()` "rejects with `EmptyError` if the source completes without emitting", whereas `.toPromise()` resolved `undefined`. It also names the affected canLoad/loadChildren paths. That is the same defect: an empty completion now becomes a rejected promise instead of a non-match. The finding is low-confidence and does not mention the recognizer catch block that only skips NoMatch errors, but it would lead a maintainer to the actual bug.
ground_truth: The PR replaces `.toPromise()` with a custom `firstValueFrom` (built on rxjs `first()`) in route recognition (`matchWithChecks`, `runCanLoadGuards`, `loadChildren`). Unlike `toPromise()`, which resolves `undefined` when an observable completes without emitting, `first()` errors with an EmptyError. Guards or matchers whose observables complete without emitting now throw EmptyError instead of being treated as "no match"; the recognizer's catch only skips NoMatch errors, so navigation fails instead of moving on to the next route. Fixed by also treating EmptyError as a non-match in recognize.ts.

findings.description: The helper is not a drop-in replacement for the previous `.toPromise()`. `toPromise()` resolved with the last emitted value, or `undefined` if the source completed empty. `first()` resolves with the first value and rejects with `EmptyError` if the source completes without emitting. An observable returned from a `redirectTo` function (or from `canLoad`/`loadChildren`) that emits several values or completes empty now behaves differently. Empty completion becomes a rejected promise, and the last value is no longer the one used. This is an edge case, and the first-value behavior is probably intended.

justification: Finding 0 states the same mechanism as the known bug. It says that `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode and "shared by every instance", and that the different-parent rule "cancels leave animations that belong to unrelated instances". In that case the element is force-removed and its leave animation is cut short. Finding 1 covers the previousSibling condition with @for, which is a different mechanism.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: `leavingNodes` is keyed by `TNode`, which is shared by every instance of a component or template. The new rule "leaving element is in a different DOM parent → cancel" therefore cancels leave animations that belong to unrelated instances. If one instance's animated root is leaving in parent P1 while another instance of the same component is inserted into parent P2 (e.g. components in different containers, or different `@for` rows), the first element is force-ended with a cancel `animationend` and removed immediately. The leave animation is cut short and the element disappears early. The diff has no way to tell the overlay/portal case apart from this one.

`cancelLeavingNodes` now runs after every insert of a node with a tracked leaving element, and it cancels whenever the leaving element is the new element's `previousSibling`. With `@for`, removing the last item (which starts a leave animation) and adding a new item in the same or a later change detection inserts the new item right after the leaving one. The leaving element then counts as the "previous sibling" and is killed abruptly. Those are different logical items, not an `@if` toggle, so the leave animation is cut short.

justification:
Finding 0 identifies the same defect as the known bug. It quotes the mechanism directly: "`leavingNodes` is keyed by `tNode`, and a `tNode` is shared by every instance". It then explains that when unrelated instance B is inserted into a different parent, the code "dispatches a cancel `animationend` and removes A's element, cutting off A's leave animation early". That is the cross-parent removal of a different logical view described in the bug.

Finding 1 concerns the previousSibling adjacency check, which is a different mechanism. Findings 2 and 3 cover memory leaks and queue removal, which are unrelated.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: The "different DOM parent" heuristic cancels and force-removes leaving elements that belong to unrelated instances. `leavingNodes` is keyed by `tNode`, and a `tNode` is shared by every instance of a component or template. If instance A is animating out in parent P1 and instance B of the same template is inserted into a different parent P2, B's insert treats A as an overlay duplicate. It dispatches a cancel `animationend` and removes A's element, cutting off A's leave animation early. This is a regression for any list of components that each have `animate.leave` and live in different containers.

`cancelLeavingNodes` runs on every Insert and cancels any leaving element that is the new node's `previousSibling`. This also fires for `@for` or ViewContainerRef cases where a different item is added right after one that is still animating out. For example, removing the last item B and then appending a new item C puts C before the anchor, directly after B. B's leave animation is then cancelled and B is removed, even though the comment says same-parent leaving items are left alone. The adjacency test cannot tell "same logical node re-created" from "unrelated new item".

On Detach, the element is added to `leavingNodes` whenever the tNode has leave animations, before `runLeaveAnimationsWithCallback` runs. If the leave animation does not run or finish normally, for example when animations are disabled or the element is removed some other way, the entry may never be cleared. That leaves stale element references that keep detached DOM alive. The `includes` check also makes each `trackLeavingNodes` call O(n).

The removal of pending enter animations from the queue when a node starts leaving has been dropped, along with `removeAnimationsFromQueue`. If a node is created and destroyed before the next animation-frame flush, its queued enter animation functions still run against an element that is already leaving or detached. This can apply enter classes or listeners to a node being removed and interfere with the leave animation.

justification: Finding 0 states that the old code sent "0,1,2" and that `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now sends "[0,1,2]". It adds that the backend's `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` still parse with `split(',')`, so they get NaN indices and view-source and select-DOM-element break. This is the same defect and mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: To escape code injected into the inspected page, the PR changes `findConstructorByPosition('${position}')` and `findDomElementByPosition('${position}')` to pass `stringifyAndEscape(position)`. `position` is an array, so it used to be serialized implicitly as a comma-separated string ("0,1,2"); now it is passed as a JSON array string ("[0,1,2]"). The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: The old code interpolated `position` (a number[]) into a quoted string, so the inspected page received the comma-separated form "0,1,2". The new `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]" instead. `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` parse their argument with `split(',')` and `parseInt`, so the bracketed form yields NaN indices ("[0" and "2]"). This breaks view-source and select-DOM-element for components. The same format change applies to `selectDomElement`.

justification: Finding 0 says the old code produced "0,1,2" and `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now yields "[0,1,2]". It notes that if `findConstructorByPosition` still splits on commas, parsing fails and "View source would then fail", and that the receiver is not updated. Finding 1 describes the same format mismatch for `findDomElementByPosition`, with the same consequence: "Selecting a DOM element from the component tree would then break." Both match the known bug's mechanism: the wire format changed while the backend consumer was left unchanged.
ground_truth: To escape code injected into the inspected page, the PR changes `findConstructorByPosition('${position}')` and `findDomElementByPosition('${position}')` to pass `stringifyAndEscape(position)`. `position` is an array, so it used to be serialized implicitly as a comma-separated string ("0,1,2"); now it is passed as a JSON array string ("[0,1,2]"). The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: The position argument changes format. Before, `'${position}'` interpolated the number[] into a string like "0,1,2". Now `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]". If `findConstructorByPosition` still parses the comma-separated form (split(',') and Number), the first and last elements become "[0" and "2]" and parse to NaN. View source would then fail to find the element. The receiving side is not updated in this diff.

`findDomElementByPosition` now receives "[0,1,2]" instead of the comma-joined "0,1,2". If it still splits on commas, the parsed indices are NaN. Selecting a DOM element from the component tree would then break. The receiving function is not updated in this diff.
